definitions.text: Not I; nor I. [Obs.]
Nigh. [Obs.] Chaucer.
See Nias.
One afflicted with nyctalopia.
Same as Nyctalopia.
The natural day and night, or space of twenty-four hours.
A South American bird of the genus Nyctibius, allied to the goatsuckers.
Turning or bending at night into special positions. drooping of the leaves, the advantage being in lessening the radiation of heat.

The tendency of certain plant organs, as leaves, to assume special "sleeping" positions or make curvatures under the influence of darkness. It is well illustrated in the leaflets of clover and other leguminous plants.
Any Australian bat of the genus Nyctophilus, having a very simple nasal appendage.
A brood or flock of pheasants.
A carnivorous mannual (Helictis moscatus, or H. orientalis), native of Eastern Asia and the Indies. It has a dorsal white stripe, and another one across the shoulders. It has a strong musky odor.

A large Asiatic antelope (Boselaphus, or Portax, tragocamelus), found in Northern India. It has short horns, a black mane, and a bunch of long hair on the throat. The general color is grayish brown. [Written also neelghau, nilgau, and nylghaie.]
(Class. Myth.)
A goddess of the mountains, forests, meadows, or waters. Where were ye, nymphs, when the remorseless deep Closed o'er the head of your loved Lycidas Milton.
Hence: A lovely young girl; a maiden; a damsel. Nymph, in thy orisons Be all my sins remembered. Shak.
(Zoöl.)
The pupa of an insect; a chrysalis.
(Zoöl.)
Any one of a subfamily (Najades) of butterflies including the purples, the fritillaries, the peacock butterfly, etc.; -- called also naiad.
(Zoöl.)
Same as Nymph, 3.
pl. (Anat.)
Two folds of mucous membrane, within the labia, at the opening of the vulva.

A genus of aquatic plants having showy flowers (white, blue, pink, or yellow, often fragrant), including the white water lily and the Egyptia lotus. be called Castalia, and the name Nymphæa transferred to what is now known as Nuphar.
Of or pertaining to a nymph or nymphs; nymphean.
An extensive family of butterflies including the nymphs, the satyrs, the monarchs, the heliconias, and others; -- called also brush-footed butterflies.
Of, pertaining to, or appropriate to, nymphs; inhabited by nymphs; as, a nymphean cave.
A little or young nymph. [Poetic] "The nymphets sporting there." Drayton.
Of or pertaining to nymphs.
Producing pupas or nymphs.
Relating to nymphs; ladylike. "Nymphish war." Drayton.
Resembling, or characteristic of, a nymph.
A species of demoniac enthusiasm or possession coming upon one who had accidentally looked upon a nymph; ecstasy. [R.] De Quincey. The nympholepsy of some fond despair. Byron.
Under the influence of nympholepsy; ecstatic; frenzied. [Poetic]
Morbid and uncontrollable sexual desire in women, constituting a true disease.
Same as Nymphomania.
Excision of the nymphæ.
Is not. See Nis. Chaucer. Spenser.
A rapid involuntary oscillation of the eyeballs.
A species of ichneumon (Herpestes nyula). Its fur is beautifully variegated by closely set zigzag markings.
